the UK government has begun to acknowledge the potential of intergenerational shared sites to support its policy objectives, and that there has been a steady increase in the number of intergenerational sites in the UK since 2012.

intergenerational shared sites in the UK are a growing phenomenon, with policy drivers including an aging population, a growing demand for services for older people, the desire to improve the quality of life for both generations and to reduce social isolation.

the ways in which intergenerational shared sites have been conceptualised and promoted by policymakers and how they are being implemented in practice.
the extent to which the UK's national and local policy agenda is beginning to recognise and acknowledge the potential of intergenerational shared sites to address contemporary challenges.
the relationship between policy and practice and, in particular, with the extent to which policy is driving practice and/or is being driven by practice.

intergenerational shared site practice has been identified by UK policymakers as a potentially valuable approach for addressing some of the key challenges faced in the delivery of public services.

while the policy landscape has been slow to recognise the value and potential of intergenerational practice, it is beginning to do so.
